blocks.text: You have spent this entire course turning messy, raw data into a clean NumPy array or a tidy pandas DataFrame. You have cleaned it, encoded it, scaled it, split it. By now that array is genuinely ready for a model. Except PyTorch and TensorFlow will not actually accept it as is.

Both frameworks compute with their own object, torch.Tensor for PyTorch and tf.Tensor for TensorFlow, not a raw NumPy array and not a pandas DataFrame. There is always one last conversion step standing between your prepared data and a model that can actually train on it. This final lesson is entirely about that last step, the actual handoff point from everything you have learned so far into real model training.

blocks.alt: A numpy array needing one more conversion step before it becomes a torch Tensor or a tf Tensor
blocks.caption: A finished NumPy array still needs one final conversion before PyTorch or TensorFlow can use it.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction: The Last Mile From Array to Tensor

It helps to be precise about why this step exists at all. A NumPy array is a block of memory with a shape and a dtype, and that is basically it. A torch.Tensor or a tf.Tensor is that same idea plus a lot more: the ability to live on a GPU, the ability to track gradients automatically during backpropagation, and deep integration with each framework own set of operations. NumPy was never built to do any of that, and it does not need to be, that was never its job.

So every deep learning pipeline, no matter how it starts, funnels down to the same narrow bridge at the end: take the finished array, hand it to the framework, get back a tensor. PyTorch gives you a couple of ways to do that, TensorFlow gives you one fairly direct equivalent, and the rest of this lesson walks through each of them along with the small details that trip people up the first time.

blocks.title: Why this is not just busywork
blocks.content: This conversion is not a formality you can skip or ignore. The dtype you carry into it, the memory behavior you pick, and the device the resulting tensor ends up on all have real consequences for whether your training run works cleanly or throws a confusing error three lines into your training loop.

blocks.text: Despite PyTorch and TensorFlow disagreeing on almost everything else, from how they build computation graphs to how they handle debugging, they agree completely on this one point: neither one will train directly on a NumPy array. That agreement is exactly why this lesson can walk through both frameworks side by side the whole way through.
2. Converting to a PyTorch Tensor

PyTorch gives you two straightforward ways to turn a NumPy array into a tensor, torch.from_numpy() and torch.tensor(). They look almost interchangeable at a glance and both hand you back a working tensor, but they behave differently underneath in a way that is genuinely worth understanding before you pick one out of habit.
2.1 torch.from_numpy: Sharing Memory

torch.from_numpy() wraps the existing NumPy array without copying its data anywhere. The resulting tensor points at the exact same block of memory the array already occupies. That makes the conversion essentially free, no matter how large the array is, since nothing gets duplicated.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import torch

arr = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
shared = torch.from_numpy(arr)
print(shared)   # tensor([1., 2., 3.], dtype=torch.float64)

blocks.text: The part that catches people off guard is what happens next. Because the tensor and the array share the same underlying memory, changing one actually changes the other, in place, with no warning.

code.content:
arr[0] = 99.0
print(shared)   # tensor([99., 2., 3.], dtype=torch.float64), it changed too
print(arr)      # [99.  2.  3.], both point at the exact same memory

blocks.alt: torch from_numpy sharing memory with the original array compared against torch.tensor making an independent copy
blocks.caption: from_numpy shares memory with the original array. torch.tensor copies it into something new and independent.

blocks.alt: Modifying a numpy array in place automatically changing the value inside its from_numpy tensor
blocks.caption: Edit the NumPy array after calling from_numpy and the tensor silently changes with it.

blocks.title: The shared memory gotcha
blocks.content: This is a real and genuinely easy mistake to make. If you preprocess an array further after wrapping it with from_numpy, or if some other part of your code still holds a reference to that original array and edits it, your tensor will change underneath you with zero errors and zero warnings. If you need a tensor that is fully independent from here on, either use torch.tensor instead or call .clone() on the shared tensor right after creating it.

blocks.text: 2.2 torch.tensor: An Independent Copy

torch.tensor() takes the opposite approach. It always allocates a brand new block of memory and copies the array data into it. The tensor you get back has no relationship to the original array at all, editing one never touches the other.

code.content:
arr = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
copied = torch.tensor(arr)

arr[0] = 99.0
print(copied)   # tensor([1., 2., 3.], dtype=torch.float64), unaffected, a real independent copy

blocks.text: That safety is not free. Copying data takes a small amount of time and a small amount of extra memory, proportional to the size of the array. For most arrays in a typical ML pipeline this cost is trivial and not worth worrying about. For a genuinely enormous array where you control both sides carefully and want to avoid any duplication, from_numpy earns its keep.
2.3 Choosing Between the Two

As a general default, reach for torch.tensor(). It is the safer choice and the copy cost is rarely something you will actually notice. Save torch.from_numpy() for cases where you specifically want zero copy behavior and you are confident nothing else in your code is going to mutate that array out from under you.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","torch.from_numpy","torch.tensor"],"rows":[["Memory","Shares the exact same memory as the NumPy array","Allocates a fresh, independent copy"],["Speed","Essentially free, no copying at all","A small copy cost, usually negligible"],["Safety","Editing one changes the other, a real gotcha","Fully isolated, editing one never touches the other"],["Typical use","Very large arrays where you want zero copy overhead and control both sides","The safer general purpose default"]]}

blocks.text: In practice, most real codebases just default to torch.tensor everywhere and only reach for from_numpy in a narrow, deliberate optimization pass once memory or speed actually becomes a measured problem, not a guess.
3. Converting to a TensorFlow Tensor

TensorFlow keeps this part simpler. There is really just one function you reach for, tf.convert_to_tensor(), and it is TensorFlow fairly direct equivalent of what torch.tensor does on the PyTorch side, it takes your NumPy array and hands you back a proper tf.Tensor.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

arr = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
tf_tensor = tf.convert_to_tensor(arr)
print(tf_tensor)   # tf.Tensor([1. 2. 3.], shape=(3,), dtype=float64)

blocks.alt: A numpy array being passed through tf.convert_to_tensor to produce a tf.Tensor
blocks.caption: tf.convert_to_tensor is TensorFlow direct, one function equivalent of the NumPy to tensor conversion.

blocks.text: You will also see tf.constant() used for the same purpose in a lot of TensorFlow code, and it behaves almost identically when you hand it a NumPy array. tf.convert_to_tensor() is the more general tool since it also happily accepts plain Python lists and existing tensors, which is why it tends to show up more often in real preprocessing code.

blocks.title: A quiet but important difference
blocks.content: Once your data becomes a tf.Tensor, it is immutable, you cannot assign into it the way you can index and reassign a NumPy array or even a torch.Tensor. TensorFlow gives you a separate object, tf.Variable, for values that genuinely need to change during training, like model weights. Your converted input data almost never needs this, tf.Tensor is exactly right for it.

blocks.text: 4. The float32 Casting Step

Back in the NumPy dtype lesson you saw that float32 is the practical default across every major deep learning framework, trading away precision you do not need for half the memory and real speed on a GPU. This is the exact point in your pipeline where that fact stops being background knowledge and starts being something you have to actively handle.

Here is the concrete problem. If you built your array the ordinary way, with plain decimal numbers and no dtype argument, NumPy defaulted it to float64. Convert that straight into a tensor and you get a float64 tensor, while the model layers you are about to feed it were built expecting float32 weights.

code.content:
arr = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])   # dtype float64 by default
print(arr.dtype)   # float64

layer = torch.nn.Linear(3, 1)   # this layer's weights default to float32
tensor = torch.tensor(arr)
output = layer(tensor)
# RuntimeError: Found dtype Double but expected Float

blocks.text: That error is the loud, obvious version. The quieter version is just as costly: some operations do not error at all, they silently upcast or keep everything running in float64, which doubles your memory footprint and slows down every single training step without ever telling you why.

blocks.alt: A float64 array causing a dtype mismatch error compared against the same array cast to float32 first and converting cleanly
blocks.caption: Converting a float64 array directly can throw a dtype error. Casting to float32 first fixes it cleanly.

blocks.text: The fix is one line, and it is worth making a habit rather than a thing you remember only after hitting the error once.

code.content:
arr32 = arr.astype('float32')
print(arr32.dtype)   # float32

tensor32 = torch.tensor(arr32)
output = layer(tensor32)   # works cleanly, no dtype mismatch

blocks.title: A very common beginner error
blocks.content: Almost everyone who starts working with PyTorch or TensorFlow hits a dtype mismatch error at some point, usually right after their first successful preprocessing pipeline, precisely because NumPy defaults to float64 and the frameworks default to float32. The exact wording of the error varies by operation and by framework, but the fix is always the same: cast to float32 with array.astype("float32") before or during the conversion, not after something has already broken.

items: Some operations raise an immediate, hard error the moment dtypes disagree.
Others silently upcast everything to float64, quietly doubling memory use with no warning at all.
A mix of float32 and float64 tensors in the same computation can also slow training down on a GPU built to run float32 fast.

blocks.text: A defensive habit worth building: check the dtype before you convert, instead of finding out only after an error three steps later.
5. NumPy and Pandas Are CPU Only: The GPU Handoff

Here is a fact worth stating plainly, because nothing earlier in this course needed you to know it: NumPy arrays and pandas DataFrames only ever live in regular system memory, on the CPU. There is no such thing as a NumPy array sitting on a GPU. That was never a limitation you needed to think about while cleaning data or engineering features, since none of that work happens on a GPU anyway.

blocks.alt: NumPy arrays and pandas DataFrames both living exclusively in CPU memory
blocks.caption: NumPy and pandas data is always CPU bound. It never touches a GPU on its own.

blocks.text: The tensor conversion you just learned is genuinely the first and only point where that changes. A torch.Tensor or a tf.Tensor can be moved onto a GPU, and once it is there, the framework can run the matrix heavy operations that make deep learning training fast. This conversion step is not just a type change, it is the actual handoff from CPU only preprocessing into GPU accelerated training.
5.1 Moving a Tensor to the GPU in PyTorch
PyTorch makes device placement explicit. A tensor starts out on the CPU by default, and you move it onto a GPU with .to, passing the device you want.

code.content:
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
tensor32 = tensor32.to(device)
print(tensor32.device)   # cuda:0 on a machine with a GPU, cpu otherwise

blocks.alt: A CPU tensor moving onto a GPU through the .to cuda call
blocks.caption: Calling .to cuda moves a tensor from CPU memory onto the GPU, the real handoff into accelerated training.

blocks.text: Checking torch.cuda.is_available() first, like the example above does, matters because your code should not assume a GPU exists. Writing it this way lets the exact same script run correctly on a laptop with no GPU and on a training server with several.

blocks.title: Getting back to NumPy later
blocks.content: Once a tensor is on a GPU, or even tracking gradients on a CPU, you cannot hand it straight back to a NumPy function. To go the other direction, call .cpu().numpy() on the tensor, which moves it back to CPU memory and converts it back into a plain NumPy array. You will use this constantly for saving predictions, plotting results, or logging metrics after training.

blocks.text: 5.2 Device Placement in TensorFlow
TensorFlow handles this more implicitly. If a compatible GPU is visible to TensorFlow, it will place a tensor on that GPU automatically without you writing any explicit device code at all.

code.content:
tf_tensor = tf.convert_to_tensor(arr32)
print(tf_tensor.device)   # points at a GPU automatically if one is visible, otherwise the CPU

blocks.text: You can still take explicit control when you want it, using a tf.device context manager to pin an operation to a specific device.

blocks.alt: PyTorch requiring an explicit .to cuda call compared against TensorFlow placing tensors on the GPU implicitly
blocks.caption: PyTorch device placement is explicit, you call .to cuda yourself. TensorFlow usually does it for you.

blocks.text: 6. What Comes Next: Dataset and DataLoader

A single tensor holding your whole dataset is not quite how real training loops consume data. Training in batches, shuffled differently every epoch, is what actually works well in practice, and PyTorch has a standard pattern built specifically for that: wrap your tensors in a Dataset, then wrap that Dataset in a DataLoader.

code.content:
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader

dataset = TensorDataset(tensor32, labels_tensor)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

for batch_features, batch_labels in loader:
    pass   # one shuffled batch of 32 examples at a time, ready for a training step

blocks.alt: Prepared tensors wrapped in a Dataset and then a DataLoader producing shuffled training batches
blocks.caption: Dataset and DataLoader turn a single tensor into shuffled, batched training data, the natural next step from here.

items: Automatic batching, so your training loop pulls fixed size chunks instead of the whole dataset at once.
Shuffling between epochs, which helps a model avoid learning the order of your data instead of the patterns in it.
Optional parallel loading with multiple worker processes, useful once your preprocessing gets heavier.

blocks.text: TensorFlow has its own version of this same idea, tf.data.Dataset, built for exactly the same job of batching and shuffling data efficiently during training. The concept transfers directly even though the API looks different.

blocks.title: Not covered in depth here, and that is fine
blocks.content: Dataset and DataLoader are genuinely their own topic, with enough detail in things like custom Dataset classes and sampler strategies to fill a lesson on their own. This course stops at the handoff point, getting your data into a clean, correctly typed tensor. Batching and training loops are the natural next place to go from here.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: One Array, Two Frameworks

Let us close the technical part of this lesson by running the whole pipeline end to end, once for PyTorch and once for TensorFlow, side by side, so the parallel between the two is completely concrete.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import torch
import tensorflow as tf

# a fully cleaned, preprocessed feature array from earlier in the pipeline
features = np.array([
    [0.42, -1.13, 2.05],
    [1.87,  0.03, -0.66],
    [-0.29, 1.44,  0.91],
])
print(features.dtype)   # float64, the numpy default

# the casting step from section 4, done once, used by both frameworks
features32 = features.astype('float32')

# PyTorch side
pytorch_tensor = torch.tensor(features32)
print(pytorch_tensor.dtype, pytorch_tensor.shape)   # torch.float32 torch.Size([3, 3])

# TensorFlow side
tensorflow_tensor = tf.convert_to_tensor(features32)
print(tensorflow_tensor.dtype, tensorflow_tensor.shape)   # <dtype: 'float32'> (3, 3)

blocks.alt: The same prepared NumPy array converting into both a PyTorch tensor and a TensorFlow tensor side by side
blocks.caption: One cleaned, casted array, two frameworks, two tensor objects, the same underlying numbers.

blocks.text: Notice what stayed the same and what changed. The numbers are identical in both tensors, the shape is identical, and the dtype is identical, float32 in both cases because you cast it once up front. What differs is only the object each framework gives you back and the function you called to get there.
8. Summary and Looking Back at the Whole Course
This is genuinely the last stop. It is worth taking a moment to look back at how far the data actually traveled to get here.

You started this course with a raw NumPy array and its single shared dtype, then learned to index it, reshape it, broadcast operations across it, and vectorize your way out of slow Python loops. From there you moved into pandas, reading real files, inspecting messy columns, filtering and sorting rows, joining and grouping tables together. Then came the harder, more judgment heavy work: imputing missing values, catching outliers, encoding categories, engineering and scaling features until the data actually looked like something a model could learn from. Every one of those steps was building toward exactly this moment, a clean, correctly typed array that a real framework can finally take off your hands.

blocks.caption: From a raw NumPy array all the way to this final handoff into GPU accelerated model training.

items: A NumPy array or pandas DataFrame is not the finish line, PyTorch and TensorFlow need their own tensor objects, torch.Tensor and tf.Tensor.

torch.tensor always makes an independent copy, a small cost for real safety, and the sensible default.
tf.convert_to_tensor is TensorFlow direct, one function equivalent for the same conversion.
NumPy defaults to float64, deep learning frameworks default to float32, and skipping an explicit .astype("float32") cast is one of the most common beginner errors there is.
NumPy and pandas data is always CPU only. The tensor conversion step is the actual handoff into GPU accelerated training.
PyTorch device placement is explicit through .to, TensorFlow usually handles it implicitly on your behalf.
Dataset and DataLoader are the natural next step after this lesson, turning a single tensor into shuffled, batched training data.

blocks.text: That is the whole arc, from a single raw array with one shared dtype all the way to a properly typed tensor handed off to a GPU. Whatever you build next, a small experiment or a full production model, it all rests on the habits this course spent so much time building: know your shapes, know your dtypes, and never assume the next tool in the chain will just figure it out for you. Congratulations on finishing the course.
